symbols.x: an input: one observed value, a query point, or (in the norm section) a vector of coordinates
symbols.y: a target (response) value; in the tutorial's matrix formulas, the whole vector of targets
symbols.bb:y: the vector of all observed target values, one per example
symbols.Y: a training example's observed response (Y_i is the i-th), averaged or weighted to make a prediction
symbols.X: a random observation (X_i is the i-th); in regression formulas, the design matrix of inputs
symbols.bar:X: the sample mean: the average of the observations (also the MLE of a mean or a proportion)
symbols.bar:x: the sample mean of x: the average of the x values
symbols.bar:y: the sample mean of y: the average of the y values
symbols.hat:y: the prediction at the query point
symbols.n: the number of samples (tutorial and lab notation)
symbols.N: the number of values in a sample (slide notation); written N(mean, variance) it is the normal distribution
symbols.m: the slides' number of samples; also the slides' sample mean (p.58, p.60) and the tutorial's trial mean
symbols.i: counts data points; in the p-norm formula it counts the coordinates of a vector
symbols.k: kNN: the number of neighbours averaged; in ridge and LASSO, the size budget on the coefficients
symbols.d: the number of features (dimensions) of the input space; in the box-car trap, a distance
symbols.p: a probability of success (Bernoulli), the exponent in a p-norm, or the density p_theta, by context
symbols.q: another exponent for a norm, compared with p
symbols.P: a probability; in the MLE setting, the unknown distribution the data are drawn from
symbols.L: the likelihood: how probable the observed data is for a candidate parameter value
symbols.cal:L: the likelihood: how probable the observed data is for a candidate parameter value
symbols.theta: the parameter being estimated; for the normal family it is (mean, variance), in regression the weights
symbols.Theta: the parameter space: the set of all allowed parameter values
symbols.hat:theta: the estimate of theta computed from data; as an estimator it varies from sample to sample
symbols.beta: the regression coefficients (the tutorial's name for theta, the same role as w)
symbols.w: the weights from Regression I (the same role as beta here)
symbols.mu: the mean of the distribution (the population mean)
symbols.hat:mu: the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean
symbols.sigma: the standard deviation of the noise or distribution; sigma squared is its variance
symbols.hat:sigma: the maximum likelihood estimate of sigma (its square divides by n, so it is biased)
symbols.s: the sample standard deviation (s squared is the sample variance, dividing by N-1)
symbols.r: the Pearson correlation: a unit-free number from -1 to +1 for linear association
symbols.lambda: the penalty strength: the price per unit of coefficient size in ridge and LASSO
symbols.alpha: a label for the constraint radius in the tutorial's figures; it is the same as k
symbols.varepsilon: random noise added to the true function; it has mean 0 and variance sigma squared
symbols.epsilon: random noise added to the true function (the tutorial's letter for it)
symbols.f: the true underlying function that the data come from, before noise
symbols.hat:f: the learned function, built from a random dataset, so it varies between datasets
symbols.bb:E: the expected value: the average over many repeated datasets
symbols.h: the bandwidth of the kernel smoother: how far its reach extends; larger h means a smoother fit
symbols.K: the kernel: turns a scaled distance into a weight (unrelated to W5's kernels)
symbols.u: the scaled distance (distance divided by h) that is fed to the kernel
symbols.cal:N: the set of the k training points nearest to the query point
symbols.D: one dataset out of the many imagined repeated datasets of the same size
symbols.T: transpose: flips a vector or matrix so rows become columns
symbols.I: the identity matrix: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere
symbols.a: a fixed constant multiplying a random quantity
symbols.g: a function being tested against the rules for a norm
symbols.C: a complexity setting from W5, mentioned as another tool against overfitting
symbols.bb:R: the set of real numbers (R squared is pairs of them)
symbols.sum: add up the term that follows, once for every value of the index shown
symbols.prod: multiply together the term that follows, once for every value of the index shown
symbols.log: the natural logarithm of the term that follows
symbols.exp: e raised to the power of the term that follows
symbols.max: the largest of the values listed
symbols.min: the smallest value the expression that follows can take
symbols.arg: the input value that gives the best score, rather than the score itself (read with max or min)
symbols.partial: the slope with respect to one variable, nudging only that one
symbols.norm: the length of the vector inside; the subscript says which rule, and a squared 2-norm is a sum of squares
symbols.abs: the size of the number inside, ignoring its sign
symbols.infty: infinity: no limit (the infinity norm is the largest coordinate size)
symbols.mid: given: what comes after the bar is known or fixed
symbols.sim: is distributed as, or is drawn from
symbols.in: is an element of, or lies in
symbols.w:var: the variance: the average squared spread around the mean; for an estimator, its spread across datasets
symbols.w:cov: the covariance: how much two variables move together
symbols.w:bias: systematic error: the average estimate minus the true value (not the bias weight or intercept)
symbols.w:variance: how much the model's prediction changes from one dataset to another
symbols.w:irreducible error: the noise error that no model can remove
symbols.w:mse: mean squared error: an estimator's average squared miss, or in the decomposition, the expected test error
symbols.w:ls: least squares: the estimate that minimises the sum of squared errors
symbols.w:bernoulli: a distribution for a yes/no outcome: 1 with probability p, otherwise 0
symbols.w:subject to: while obeying the condition that follows
symbols.w:is a knn of: is one of the k nearest neighbours of
symbols.hat:p: the maximum likelihood estimate of p: the proportion of successes in the data

The big picture.m: the slides' number of samples (and, on p.58 and p.60, their sample mean); the tutorial uses n

Estimation and unbiasedness.i: counts the values in the sample
Estimation and unbiasedness.m: the sample mean, the slides' letter for it on p.58 and p.60 (not a count)

Covariance and correlation.x: the observed values of the first variable
Covariance and correlation.y: the observed values of the second variable

Maximum likelihood estimation.N: the normal (Gaussian) distribution, written with its mean and variance
Maximum likelihood estimation.P: the unknown distribution the observations are drawn from
Maximum likelihood estimation.p: the density p_theta in the setting; in the results table, a Bernoulli success probability
Maximum likelihood estimation.theta: the parameters of the assumed family; for the normal family, (mean, variance)
Maximum likelihood estimation.X: a random observation; X_i is the i-th of the independent draws

Tutorial Q1(a).m: a trial value of the mean, tried in place of mu
Tutorial Q1(a).N: the normal (Gaussian) distribution, written with its mean and variance

Tutorial Q1(b).P: the probability of the outcome shown

Tutorial Q1(c).m: a trial value of the mean, tried in place of mu
Tutorial Q1(c).s: a trial standard deviation: s squared stands in for the variance sigma squared

Bias and variance of an estimator.theta: the true value of the quantity being estimated
Bias and variance of an estimator.N: the normal (Gaussian) distribution, written with its mean and variance
Bias and variance of an estimator.p: the probability of success for Bernoulli data
Bias and variance of an estimator.X: a random observation; X_i is the i-th of the independent draws
Bias and variance of an estimator.bb:E: the average over many repeated datasets of the same size
Bias and variance of an estimator.w:mse: the estimator's mean squared error: its average squared miss from the true value

Tutorial Q2(a,b).p: the probability of success for Bernoulli data

Tutorial Q2(c).N: the normal (Gaussian) distribution, written with its mean and variance
Tutorial Q2(c).T: an example estimator: 0.8 times the sample mean
Tutorial Q2(c).w:mse: the estimator's mean squared error: its average squared miss from the true value

The probabilistic view of least squares.X: the design matrix: one row per example, one column per feature
The probabilistic view of least squares.P: the probability (density) of the targets given the inputs and the weights
The probabilistic view of least squares.y: the target value for an example, or the whole vector of targets in matrix form
The probabilistic view of least squares.m: the number of samples (slide notation; the tutorial uses n)
The probabilistic view of least squares.N: the normal (Gaussian) distribution, written with its mean and variance
The probabilistic view of least squares.theta: the regression weights (the slides' name; the tutorial uses beta)
The probabilistic view of least squares.j: counts the data points (slide notation; the tutorial uses i)
The probabilistic view of least squares.i: counts the data points (tutorial notation; the slides use j)

p-norms.p: the exponent that picks which norm rule is used
p-norms.x: a vector, written as a list of coordinates
p-norms.i: counts the coordinates of the vector
p-norms.norm: the length of the vector under the rule the subscript names
p-norms.g: a function being tested for the three norm rules
p-norms.c: any fixed constant that scales a vector

Ridge and LASSO as constrained.k: the size budget on the coefficients (unrelated to the k of kNN)
Ridge and LASSO as constrained.alpha: the tutorial's inconsistent label for the same budget k
Ridge and LASSO as constrained.lambda: the price of coefficient size in the penalised form; larger lambda matches a smaller k
Ridge and LASSO as constrained.norm: the size of the coefficient vector; ridge charges the squared 2-norm, LASSO the plain 1-norm

Definitions.w:bias: the model's average prediction at a point minus the true value there
Definitions.w:variance: how much the prediction at a point changes from one dataset to another
Definitions.bb:E: the average over many possible training datasets

The decomposition.bb:E: the average over many training datasets and noise draws
The decomposition.w:mse: the expected squared error of a prediction at a new point
The decomposition.w:var: the variance: for f-hat, how much its prediction changes between datasets; for epsilon, the noise variance

kNN regression.k: the number of nearest neighbours that are averaged: the complexity dial
kNN regression.X: a training point's input; X_i is the i-th
kNN regression.i: counts training points; the sum picks only those among the k nearest

Linear smoothing.X: a training point's input; X_i is the i-th
Linear smoothing.j: counts all training points in the weights' total
Linear smoothing.norm: the distance between the query point and a training point

The curse of dimensionality.d: the number of features (dimensions) of the points
The curse of dimensionality.n: the number of random points sampled

Code you should recognise.d: the polynomial degree: the highest power of x added as a feature
Code you should recognise.x: the single input column that the powers are built from

Exam traps.d: the distance from the query point to a training point (so u = d divided by h)
Exam traps.k: kNN: the number of neighbours (small k is complex); in the budget, the coefficient size limit
Exam traps.p: a Bernoulli probability, or the exponent of a p-norm, by context
